prime.problem: Starting with Attention Is All You Need leaves Q, K and V floating: the paper assumes you already know what a token is, where its vector comes from, what the model outputs and how one output becomes the next input. Without that route in your head, every later paper is a box with no arrows going in or out.
prime.fits: This is the spine of the course. Each of its ten stops links to the course card or hub card that teaches it in depth, so read it first and come back to it after each deeper card.
expect: the loop that appends one token at a time
prime.goal: Trace any input from text to generated answer, give the shape of the data at every stop, and say which paper explains each stop.

attend: Why are there 7 tokens for 29 characters, and what decides where the cuts fall?
The embedding table is used twice in this model. Where is the second time, and what does it turn the last vector into?
If there is no position table, where does Qwen put word order back in?
Which steps of the greedy answer were uncertain, and why is ␣Delhi at 0.994 once ␣New has been chosen?
On the step after The capital of India is, why does top-p 0.9 keep 5 tokens while top-k 2 keeps 2?

must: Text is cut by learned merges (BPE) → each piece is an integer ID → the ID selects one row of the embedding table → the model only ever works with those vectors, never with letters, which is why spelling and digits behave oddly
Attention mixes tokens but ignores order → order has to be put back (Qwen rotates Q and K with RoPE in every layer) → without it, India of capital would look the same as capital of India

One block = attention (tokens read earlier tokens) + feed-forward (each token alone), each added back through a residual → the block repeats 24 times with the shape fixed at tokens × 896 → only the last position's vector becomes the 151,936 logits

Logits → softmax → a decoder picks one token → it is appended and the model runs again → the answer's probability is the product of each step's choice (≈ 0.11 here) → the decoder, not the model, decides whether you get the safe answer or a strange one
elevated: The embedding table is also the output layer (tied weights) → it holds 136M of the 494M parameters (27.6%) → in a small model the vocabulary is a big share of the size

Pure sampling keeps the whole tail → about 0.09 of the probability sat below the top-p 0.9 cut on one step → over a dozen steps sampling lands in the tail often, which is why the four sampled answers wandered off
reference: Qwen2.5-0.5B: 24 layers, hidden 896, 14 query heads, 2 KV heads, head dim 64, FFN 4,864 (SwiGLU), vocab 151,936 rows (151,665 real tokens)
the paper per stop: BPE (Sennrich 2015), SentencePiece, word2vec, RoFormer, ALiBi, Attention Is All You Need, MQA, GQA, FlashAttention 1–2, Switch Transformers, GPT-3, Holtzman et al. 2019

compress.prompt: Card closed, draw the route as one line of arrows from text to answer and write the data's shape under each arrow for our 7-token question. Then add one sentence on where order enters and one on what makes it a loop.
checklist: order is added inside attention by RoPE, not by a separate table
attention + feed-forward, repeated 24 times; the shape stays 7 × 896
last vector → 151,936 logits → softmax → a decoder picks one token
the token is appended and the model runs again until end-of-text

retrieve.q: Explain why reading Attention Is All You Need first is harder than following one input through the model first.
answer: the paper assumes tokens, embeddings, softmax and decoding
it describes a 2017 encoder-decoder translation model, not today's decoder-only LLMs
following one input gives each stop an input and an output you can check, so Q, K and V attach to something concrete

retrieve.q: Walk the token ␣India from the moment the text is typed until it influences the next-token logits. Name each stop and what it does to the data.
answer: the tokenizer emits the piece ␣India (leading space included) with ID 6747
row 6747 of the 151,936 × 896 table becomes its vector
in each of 24 blocks, later tokens' queries read its key and value (with RoPE encoding its position), and the feed-forward rewrites its vector
its information reaches the last position through attention; only the last vector is projected to logits

retrieve.q: On the step after The capital of India is, choose a decoder for (a) a factual Q&A service and (b) brainstorming city names. Justify each with the card's numbers.
answer: (a) greedy or a low temperature: ␣New is 0.698, and T = 0.7 lifts it to 0.869; beam search with 4 beams gave the same answer
(b) top-p around 0.9: keeps 5 tokens, so there is variety but the 0.09 tail is cut
pure sampling (no cut) wandered off on all 4 seeds

retrieve.q: The base model gave its first answer token only 0.277. Why so low, and would a chat model behave differently?
answer: a base model only continues text: after a question it may answer, repeat or ask another question (␣The, ␣India, ␣What)
a chat model is fine-tuned on a template where an answer follows the question, so its first token is far more certain
the route is identical; only the weights differ

compare.q: That card cuts a code-token distribution at p = 0.95 and keeps 5 tokens. Here p = 0.9 also keeps 5. What does that say about how top-p sizes its set, and what would top-k 5 do on each?
answer: top-p sets the size by cumulative probability, so the count depends on how peaked the distribution is
here two tokens hold 0.862 and three small ones close the gap to 0.9
top-k 5 keeps 5 in both cases whatever the shape, including tokens the model barely believes in

compare.q: nanoGPT adds a learned position vector to each token vector. Qwen has no position table. What does each one do, and what does RoPE gain?
answer: nanoGPT: wte[id] + wpe[pos], added once at the input, limited to the trained length
Qwen: rotates Q and K in every attention layer by an angle set by the position
after the rotation the dot product depends on the distance between tokens, which carries over to longer inputs better

predict.q: Imagine the same model with a 32,000-entry vocabulary instead of 151,936, everything else unchanged. Which stops change shape, and what happens to the embedding table's share of the parameters? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: Stop 3's table becomes 32,000 × 896 = 28,672,000 weights, and stop 7 produces 32,000 logits instead of 151,936. The model shrinks to 386,570,112 parameters, and the table's share falls from 27.6% to about 7.4%. The blocks don't change at all. The catch: with fewer merges, the same text usually splits into more tokens, so every later stop runs on a longer input.

apply.task: Using only the card's step-9 probabilities (␣New 0.698, ␣Delhi 0.164, ␣known 0.018, ␣Mumbai 0.015, ␣not 0.013): (1) apply top-k 3 and give the rescaled probabilities; (2) apply top-p 0.8 and say how many tokens survive and with what probabilities. Then run labs/the-whole-route.py with a question of your own and note which steps of its greedy answer fall below 0.9.
apply.done: Top-k 3 gives 0.793 / 0.186 / 0.020 (dividing by 0.880). Top-p 0.8 keeps 2 tokens, because 0.698 + 0.164 = 0.862 ≥ 0.8, rescaled to 0.810 and 0.190. For your own question you have a list of the uncertain steps.
apply.hint: Rescaling means dividing each kept probability by the sum of the kept ones.
